Set-level F1 is non-linear and admits no closed-form threshold rule \cite{dembczynski2011exact}. We use balanced linear utility ($\alpha{=}1$ throughout); balanced set-overlap and F1 induce similar optimal thresholds for typical NER output sizes ($|E_\cup| \leq 30$).

\paragraph{Practical implications.}
The cascade provides a pre-deployment diagnostic: measure degeneracy and LP-F1 alignment on a held-out set before investing in $N{\times}$ inference.
When degeneracy exceeds $\theta_{\text{crit}}{=}0.70$, aggregation is unlikely to help; when both conditions are favorable ($D{<}22\%$, LP $\rho{>}0.2$), entity-level construction offers modest but reliable gains.
The gap between oracle scaling ($R^2{>}0.999$; \S\ref{sec:scaling}) and realized gains (${\leq}1.4$\,pp) suggests that inference-time scaling for structured prediction requires fundamentally different strategies from discrete-answer tasks---entity-level rather than sample-level aggregation, and quality-aware weighting rather than majority vote.
